summary: PULSE (Physiological Universal Life Support Engine) is an offline-first health monitoring and decision-support system for astronauts on missions where contact with Earth is delayed or lost. It builds a personal baseline for each crew member from wearable and manual data, then detects drifts and shared exposures across the whole crew (for example a slow CO₂ build-up). Findings are passed to a local medical LLM with retrieval over a curated knowledge base. The assistant explains results in plain language, guides crew through validated protocols, suggests the next most informative test, and prepares structured consult packets for ground doctors. Safety-critical alarms come from a deterministic rules engine, never from the LLM alone. Missing days and sensor failures are handled by design: data can be back-filled without loss, and a gamified interface rewards honest reporting instead of good health scores. PULSE adapts its behaviour to the link delay, from live consult to assisted autonomy.
details:
What it does. PULSE acts as an on-board “family doctor” for astronauts who are not physicians and have very little spare time. A daily check-in takes about one minute, wearable and environmental sensors add data passively, and the system decides which extra test, if any, is worth the crew member’s time that day.

How it works.

  1. An append-only event log stores every measurement with its measurement time, recording time, source and quality, so missing days can be back-filled and nothing is ever overwritten.
  2. A deterministic analysis layer builds robust personal baselines that handle irregular sampling, detects slow drifts (EWMA/CUSUM), runs a rules engine for alarms, and looks for drifts shared by several astronauts that correlate with environmental variables such as CO₂ and space weather.
  3. A vector database holds clinical cards and protocols on spaceflight health risks, retrieved by describing the pattern of change.
  4. A local medical LLM MedGemma receives structured findings rather than raw numbers. It cites the cards, states its confidence, can raise but never lower an alarm set by the rules, and says when it does not know, preparing an SBAR consult packet for ground doctors.
  5. A store-and-forward sync with a link simulator changes the system’s behaviour as delay grows, from live consult to assisted autonomy.
  6. The interface shows a traffic-light status, trends, chat and an emergency mode. The gamification rewards complete and honest reporting (declared skips count, streaks never reset, time is saved when data is reliable) and never rewards health values, because astronauts are known to under-report symptoms.

Why it matters. On Mars, one-way communication delays reach about 22 minutes, and blackouts are possible. Crews will need continuous, low-burden monitoring and decision support that stays safe when ground doctors cannot answer. The same approach applies to remote clinics, polar stations and ships.

What is creative. Crew-level detection of shared exposures; adaptive test selection that minimises time burden; resilience to missing, wrong or biased data; an autonomy mode tied to link delay; honesty-oriented game design.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, SQLite, Chroma, Ollama with MedGemma, React, Recharts.

Data. All astronaut data is synthetic, generated by our own simulator for five scenarios (for example crew-wide CO₂ exposure, a single infection, a blackout with back-fill). Clinical knowledge cards are based on public NASA sources and have not been clinically validated.

Use of SI. Code, documentation and parts of the knowledge base were drafted with the help of Claude (Anthropic) through an AI coding agent, and reviewed by the team. The in-app assistant uses MedGemma by Google. No NASA branding was generated or modified.

Limitations. PULSE is a research prototype, not a medical device. It supports decisions and does not diagnose. Thresholds and clinical content require expert review before any real use.
